text_summary.body: The book names no author in a heading. Chapters 1–6 tell of Daniel and his companions in the third person; chapters 7–12 report Daniel's visions largely in the first person; 7:1 says he wrote the dream down, and 8:26 and 12:4, 9 speak of sealing the vision or book until the time of the end. 2:4b–7:28 is in Aramaic, the rest in Hebrew.

setting.period: Narrative setting 605–536 BC; proposed composition dates range from the late sixth century to c. 164 BC
setting.body: The question was already argued in antiquity: Porphyry (3rd century AD) held the book was written under Antiochus Epiphanes and narrated past events, and Eusebius, Apollinaris and Methodius replied (Jerome). Modern critical scholarship (Driver; Montgomery) dates the final composition, at least of chs. 7–12, to 168–164 BC; conservative scholarship (Wilson; Pusey, Hengstenberg and others not read here) defends composition by Daniel in the sixth century. A Qumran copy, 4QDanᶜ (4Q114), has a radiocarbon range of 230–160 BCE (Popović et al. 2025).

terminology.gloss: Attribution of a work to an earlier figure; on the critical view, the visions are written in Daniel's name in the second century.
"Prophecy after the event" — the critical description of the historical survey of ch. 11 up to 11:39.

competing_reconstructions.label: Sixth century BC, by Daniel (traditional)
proponents: R. D. Wilson (1917): a date "say 535 B.C." remains tenable
K. A. Kitchen (1965), T. C. Mitchell & R. Joyce (1965): the language does not exclude an early date
competing_reconstructions.summary: Scholarly arguments: the linguistic evidence cannot decide the date (Kitchen; Mitchell & Joyce); alleged historical errors rest on silence and on mistaken assumptions about regnal reckoning (Wilson); Babylonian details such as Belshazzar's kingship fit a writer close to events (Wilson); Josephus reports the book shown to Alexander (Ant. 11.8.5); the radiocarbon range of 4Q114 begins before the Maccabean crisis. Theological commitments (stated separately): Jesus calls Daniel a prophet (Matt 24:15; Mark 13:14); predictive prophecy is possible; Baldwin (via Guzik) argues that a late date would make the visions fiction.

competing_reconstructions.label: Final composition c. 167–164 BC (critical)
competing_reconstructions.summary: Scholarly arguments: Greek instrument names (3:5) and Persian loanwords; the book stands among the Writings, not the Prophets; Ben Sira (c. 200 BC) omits Daniel; detailed accuracy in ch. 11 to the persecution of Antiochus, then divergence at 11:40–45; developed angelology and resurrection; historical difficulties (Dan 1:1, Belshazzar as king, Darius the Mede). Theological stance (stated separately): Driver held that a late date does not deny the book's religious value.

competing_reconstructions.label: Two stages: tales of chs. 1–6 in the 3rd century (Babylonia); visions of chs. 7–12 in 168–165 BC
competing_reconstructions.summary: The stories are pre-Maccabean, compiled from Jewish and Babylonian traditions after the Diadochi; the four visions were written seriatim in the first years of the Maccabean revolt. Montgomery notes he broke with the view that the whole book is Maccabean.

commentary.paraphrase: Guzik describes the critical view of ch. 11 as history written after the fact and quotes Baldwin that on that view the vision of ch. 10 would also be fiction.

open_questions: Wilson's promised philological volume and Pusey (1864) not read.
The relation of Ezekiel's "Daniel" (Ezek 14:14; 28:3) to the book's hero (review open).

not_applicable.locations: Place of composition is itself disputed (Babylonia or Judaea).
